title: Part One, Chapter 7: Sipacua and the Four Hundred Boys

verses.t: And here go the deeds of Sipacua, the first son of Vucub-caquix. "I am the maker of the mountains," says Sipacua. And this Sipacua was bathing in a river when the four hundred boys passed by, dragging a log for a pillar of their house, four hundred all together; they had cut a great tree for the main beam of their thatched house. And when Sipacua saw this, he went to where the four hundred boys were and asked them, "And what are you doing, boys?" "This log," they answered, "we cannot lift it." "Lift it? I shall carry it," said Sipacua. "And where is it to go? What is it for, or why have you cut it?" "For the main beam of our house," they answered. "Very well," said Sipacua, and pulling at it, he loaded it on his back and carried it to the door of the house of the four hundred boys. And then they said to him, "Stay with us. Do you have a mother or father?" "I have none," answered Sipacua. "Tomorrow," said the four hundred boys, "we shall go back to fetch another log for a pillar of our house." "Good," said Sipacua. And the four hundred boys went into council and said, "What shall we do with this boy? Let us kill him, for what he does is not good; he lifted the log all by himself. This is what we shall do: we shall make a great pit and throw him down into it. We shall say to him, 'Go and take the earth out of that pit,' and when he is bent over in the pit, we shall throw a great log down on him, and he will die there in the pit." And then they made a great, very deep pit; then they called Sipacua and said to him, "We are your friends; go and dig a little more in the pit, because we cannot reach." "Very well," he said, and went down into the pit. "Dig well," they told him, "until you make it very deep." "Very well," he said, and then he began to dig. But the hole he made was for his own escape, because he knew that they wanted to kill him; and he dug a hole to one side, an arm's length of tunnel, in which he saved himself. "Is it dug yet? Is it deep yet?" the boys said to him. "I am still digging; I shall let you know and call you when the pit is dug," said Sipacua down below in the pit. But he was not digging the bottom of the pit for his burial, but a hole in which to save himself. And afterwards Sipacua called from down below (but he had already escaped when he called): "Come, take away the earth that has been dug out at the bottom of the pit, for truly I have dug very deep. Do you not hear my voice? I hear your echo and I hear your voice, though I am in a pit with two turns," said Sipacua in his hole; and he was crouching there and shouting often. And then the boys dragged the log and threw it with a crash down into the pit, and they said, "Silence, everyone! Let no one speak; let us listen for him to scream." And they spoke in whispers among themselves, and then they threw the log into the pit; and when he gave a cry, the log fell. And then they rejoiced and said, "Oh, how well we have done! He is dead now; and if he had lived he would have done us much harm, because he had already got in among us, the four hundred boys." And they said, rejoicing, "Now what we shall do is make our chicha in these three days, and after the three days we, the four hundred boys, shall drink our chicha. Tomorrow we shall see, and the day after tomorrow we shall see, whether the ants come in the earth when he stinks and rots; and then our hearts will be at rest, and we shall drink without a care," they said. And Sipacua heard it all in the hole, when the boys spoke. And then on the second day the ants came out in swarms; they went about and multiplied and came under the log, and some carried hair and some carried the nails of Sipacua. And when the boys saw it they said, "That demon has perished now. Look at the ants: they came and gathered, and they are all carrying hair and nails. Look what we have done!" But Sipacua was alive; he had cut his nails and the hair of his head himself, biting off his nails with his mouth and giving them to the ants. And so the four hundred boys thought that he had died. And on the third day the drinking began, and the boys got drunk; and when all the four hundred boys were drunk and senseless, then the house was brought down upon their heads by Sipacua, and they were all crushed; not one, not two of the four hundred boys escaped. They were killed by Sipacua, the son of Vucub-caquix. And such were the deaths of the four hundred boys. And so it is said that they went to take the place of the Pleiades in the sky, which are called "motz," that is, a heap, because they were killed in a heap. And this, perhaps, will be a lie. Now we shall tell how Sipacua was defeated by those two boys, Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque.
